items.title: Using a lookup-table to correct an approximation
items.content:
I often find myself writing (by which I mean generating) functions to convert enums to strings. A naïve implementation of such a function might look like:

Compiling the above with a modern gcc at -O0 or -O1 gives some fairly horrible assembly code. Thankfully, at -O2 and above, a modern gcc can rewrite it to something more along the lines of:

The assembly code for this is much nicer, although the table of pointers still takes up more space than I'd like (and that's before you account for each table entry needing a relocation entry...). It can be made smaller by concatenating all the strings together into a single contiguous piece of memory and then using a table of offsets into that memory, taking advantage of the fact that a relative offset can be much smaller than a pointer:

This is pretty good, but the offsets table can be made even smaller. Consider the function x ↦ offsets[x] : it maps 0 to 0 and 22 to 382 , so one possible linear approximation of this could be x ↦ x * int(round(382.0 / 22.0)) , also known as x ↦ x * 17 . It is rarely the case that x * 17 exactly equals offsets[x] , but the difference between x * 17 and offsets[x] happens to always end up being in the range [-9, +10] . As such, the offsets table can be replaced with x * 17 and a table of corrections, where the corrections table occupies less space than the original offsets table:

There's a general pattern here: an exact function can be computed via a fast but incorrect approximation followed by a table of corrections, and doing so can be profitable if this allows a smaller table than other approaches would require. This is not a novel idea, but it still needs repeating from time to time, even if only to remind compiler developers that there are still optimisations they're missing.

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: DHS Said They Searched Man Who Wiped GrapheneOS Phone for Child Abuse Material. They Lied
items.content:
When a Department of Homeland Security official sent out an alert to stop Samuel Tunick, a Stop Cop City activist, at an airport in January 2025, they said the reason was because he was suspected of “terrorist activities,” according to new filed court records which include a screenshot of the alert and photos of Tunick’s interrogation.

Tunick ultimately provided Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officials with a code that, when entered, wiped his security- and privacy-focused GrapheneOS phone. Tunick is now being criminally charged for that alleged act, in one of the most high profile technology civil rights cases in recent memory.

The court records also showed that CBP officials lied to Tunick during his interrogation. Instead of saying he was being targeted for suspected terrorism — although this search happened just at the start of the second Trump administration, it has dramatically broadened what organizations or people may be considered such — they said they needed his phone to look for “kiddie porn.”

“Good afternoon,” an email sent from a Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) official, part of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), to CBP and other officials reads. “The following subject is scheduled to arrive in ATL [Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport] today via DL 1778 @ 1930 Hours. TUNICK is under investigation by HSI/JTTF for suspected terrorist activities.” The email includes a photo of Tunick, and asks the officials to direct him to secondary inspection, retain all of his electronics, and collect their passcodes.

Image: screenshot of the court document. As 404 Media first revealed in December , Tunick was charged because he allegedly “did knowingly destroy, damage, waste, dispose of, and otherwise take any action to delete the digital contents of a Google Pixel cellular phone, for the purpose of preventing and impairing the Government’s lawful authority to take said property into its custody and control.” Matthew Dodge, one of Tunick’s lawyers, previously told 404 Media he only found one other case using the same obscure law, a drug trafficking case. “This is extraordinarily rare,” Dodge said.

Tunick was part of the Stop Cop City movement in Atlanta, which broadly protested the building of a large police training center, and which authorities investigated for arson, vandalism, and doxing. Tunick is not suspected of any crime beyond the alleged wiping of the phone, and has previously put his current prosecution in the context of the wide spanning cases against other Stop Cop City protesters.

Images: screenshots of the court document.

The newly filed court record , in which Tunick’s lawyers argue that evidence should be thrown out, include new photos and descriptions of the airport encounter. The CBP officials asked Tunick if they were going to find “kiddie porn” on his phone, which Tunick immediately denied. “As the evidentiary hearing made clear, these unfounded accusations were nothing more than pretext for a fishing expedition into the depths of Mr. Tunick’s devices,” the lawyers wrote. They added, “Officer Findley acknowledged that officers had no reason whatsoever to believe Mr. Tunick possessed child pornography,” referring to one of the officials.

Tunick faces a maximum of five years in federal prison for allegedly wiping the phone.

“I hope people understand that the charges against me are meant to intimidate people against protecting their data and their privacy, and the government hopes to set a precedent that no one has the right to privacy,” Tunick previously told 404 Media.

Joseph is an award-winning investigative journalist focused on generating impact. His work has triggered hundreds of millions of dollars worth of fines, shut down tech companies, and much more.

items.title: I built a self-hosted platform for vibe-coded apps, with IT in control. Here’s how it went
items.content:
Self-hosted hosting for the apps your team builds with Claude Code. items.title: 사생활침해 범죄가 의심 됩니다. 도움이 필요합니다
items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

개별 이미지들의 위치 변경, 삭제, 별칭 추가, 폴더명 변경을 할 수 있습니다
